newsitem.title: USA: Mass. House expected to pass $18.3 bln budget.
newsitem.headline: Mass. House expected to pass $18.3 bln budget.

text.p: The Massachusetts House of Representatives is expected to pass a $18.3 billion budget by week's end, including approval of a $3.9 billion transportation bond.

House budget writers agreed with Weld's call to accelerate planned payments to reduce the unfunded liability in the state's pension fund. While state Treasurer Joe Malone suggested that the state should continue on its 30-year plan to cut that debt to make money available for the Central Artery/Third Harbor Tunnel project, the House is like to agree to reduce the debt over 20 years.

Moving at a near-record pace for such a major bill, the House last week passed a $3.9 billion bond authorization that had cleared the Transportation Committee a week earlier. The combined federal and state dollars would be used over the next two years to fund projects upgrading the state's transportation network. More than $2 billion of the money would go to the Central Artery Project.

A day after the bill left the Transportation Committee on April 2, it was stamped by the House's new Long Term Debt and Capital Expenditures Committee. Last Tuesday, it surfaced from the House Ways and Means Committee and was whisked through the House the next day.

The Senate side appears to be just as eager to process the bill quickly. The Senate Ways and Means Committee plans an executive session this week to ready the bond for action by the full Senate on Thursday.
The particulars will eventually end up in a House-Senate conference committee.
Meanwhile, no action is expected this week on a $685 million bond authorization to upgrade the state's courthouses and add new facilities.
The six House and Senate conferees, who were sent differing version of the bill earlier this year, are likely preoccupied with debate over other fiscal 1998 spending priorities.

The bill was passed on a stepped-up schedule early this year because legislative leaders said it was so badly needed, but bogged down after the Senate included some projects the House leadership had not expected.

And the Banks and Banking Committee is expected on Tuesday to deal with several bills concering the practice of charging user fees at automated teller machines. Some of the bills would prohibit the practice outright, while other simply require the banks to disclose that a fee is being charged.

Among other the items that are to be debated by the full House - an increase in the income-tax deduction for dependent children, which enjoys wide support among both Republicans and Democrats, and picking up the cost of some benefits the federal government is taking away from legal immigrants.
